title: Amyraut's providence in good acts: presenting the object and disposing the subject
source_text: XLIX. Veruntamen praeter istum concursum generalem agnoscit magnam esse providentiae Dei efficaciam, qua actus voluntatis nostrae tam bonos, quam malos & indifferentes, conformiter suo aeterno decreto in tempore determinat. Sed totam illam divinae providentiae efficacitatem, quae sese in bono exerit, reducit ad duos actus, nempe ad objecti propositionem, quam libertatem nihil violare manifestum est. Deinde ad internam subjecti dispositionem, quae in eo consistit, ut facultates liberentur ab impedimentis, quae ad nativam eorum constitutionem accesserunt, aut etiam supra naturae sortem aliquo modo evehantur, qua in re non minus evidens est hominis libertati nihil praejudicari.
pass_a_gloss: Nevertheless besides that general concurrence he acknowledges that there is a great efficacy of the providence of God, by which he determines in time the acts of our will as well good, as evil and indifferent, conformably to his eternal decree. But all that efficacy of divine providence, which shows itself in good, he reduces to two acts, namely to the proposition of the object, which it is manifest violates liberty in nothing. Then to the internal disposition of the subject, which consists in this, that the faculties be freed from the impediments, which have come upon their native constitution, or even be in some way raised above the lot of nature, in which matter it is no less evident that nothing is prejudiced to the liberty of man.
pass_b_english: Even so, besides that general concurrence Amyraut recognizes a great efficacy of God's providence, by which God determines in time the acts of our will, good, bad and indifferent alike, in keeping with his eternal decree.

But he reduces the whole efficacy of divine providence that shows itself in good acts to two operations. The first is the presenting of the object, which plainly does no violence to freedom. The second is the inner disposing of the subject, which consists in freeing the faculties from the hindrances that have come upon their native constitution, or even in raising them in some way above the lot of nature. Here too it is no less evident that human freedom suffers no prejudice.

lemmas.gloss: the internal disposition of the subject

choices.why: The Schools' term for God's acting together with secondary causes; 'concurrence' keeps it recognizable as the technical term, with 'cooperation' kept for cooperatio.
